Understanding Afro-Textured Hair, Moisture and a Safe Workstation

Before you braid a single row, you need to understand why afro-textured hair is beautiful but fragile, how it loses and keeps moisture, and how to set up tools that will not spread infection. This module gives you that foundation, with a simple wash-day routine and a hygiene system you will use for every client.

Most women in this course will work on **afro-textured hair**: hair that grows in tight coils, zig-zags and spirals. It is the most common hair type in Nigeria and across Africa. It is not "hard" or "bad" hair. It simply has a shape that needs a particular kind of care. Once you understand the shape, many everyday problems like breakage, dryness and thin edges start to make sense.

What a single strand is made of

Each hair grows from a **follicle**, a small pocket in the skin of the scalp. The part you can see is dead protein called **keratin**, so hair cannot heal itself once it is damaged. A strand has three layers:

**Cuticle**: the outer layer of flat, overlapping scales, like roof tiles. When the scales lie flat, hair looks shiny and holds water. When they are lifted or broken, hair feels rough and loses moisture fast.
**Cortex**: the thick middle layer that gives hair its strength, elasticity and colour. Relaxers and bleach work by changing the cortex, which is why they can weaken hair.
**Medulla**: a soft core found in some thicker hairs. It does not matter much for everyday care.

The scalp also makes a natural oil called **sebum**. On straight hair, sebum slides down the strand easily. On tightly coiled hair, it struggles to travel past each bend, so the ends stay dry even when the scalp feels oily. This is one main reason afro-textured hair needs regular moisture from outside.
Why coils break

Every bend in a coil is a weak point. When hair is combed dry, pulled tight or brushed hard, the strand snaps at those bends. Coils also wrap around each other and form knots, especially at the ends. That is why gentle detangling, moisture and low tension are the three rules you will hear again and again in this course.
Curl pattern and porosity

Many stylists use a simple typing chart made popular by the hairstylist Andre Walker: type 1 is straight, type 2 wavy, type 3 curly and type 4 coily. Type 4 is split into 4A (springy S-shaped coils), 4B (sharper Z-shaped bends) and 4C (very tight coils that shrink a lot). One head can have two or three patterns, often tighter at the nape and looser at the crown. Use the chart as a quick language with clients, not as a strict rule.

**Porosity** describes how easily water gets into the hair and stays there. The popular "float test" (dropping a strand into a cup of water) is not reliable, because products and oils on the hair change the result. A better check is to watch how hair behaves on wash day: how fast it gets wet, how long it takes to dry, and how quickly it feels dry again after moisturising.
Hair grows in a cycle

Each follicle goes through a growing phase that lasts years, a short resting phase, and then the old hair sheds so a new one can grow. Losing some hairs every day is normal. When a client takes down braids after six weeks, she will see a ball of shed hair, because the hairs that shed during those weeks were trapped in the braids. Explain this calmly so she does not panic.

Clean, moisturised hair is easier to style, breaks less and gives neater braids. A good wash day is the foundation of every service you will sell. Many stylists and dermatologists suggest washing afro-textured hair about once every one to two weeks, adjusting for sweat, dandruff and the style being worn. Washing every day strips the little sebum the hair has.

The wash-day order
**Pre-poo (optional)**: apply oil or conditioner to dry hair for 15 to 30 minutes before washing to reduce tangles and protect the ends.
**Section**: divide the hair into four to six sections with clips or loose twists. Working in sections prevents matting.

**Shampoo the scalp**: focus shampoo on the scalp with the pads of your fingers, not your nails. Let the lather run down the length. A sulphate-free shampoo is gentler for regular use; a clarifying shampoo removes build-up but is drying, so use it occasionally.
**Condition**: apply conditioner to the length and ends. Leave it on for the time on the label.
**Detangle while conditioner is in**: use fingers first, then a wide-tooth comb, starting at the ends and working up to the roots.
**Rinse with cool or lukewarm water**, then blot with a cotton T-shirt or microfibre towel instead of rubbing.
**Moisturise and seal** with the LOC or LCO method, then stretch the hair in twists or braids if you will style later.

**Deep conditioning** every two to four weeks gives extra softness. Apply a thick conditioner or hair mask, cover with a plastic cap, and leave for 15 to 30 minutes. Gentle warmth from a warm towel or hooded dryer helps it work, especially on low porosity hair.
LOC and LCO: moisture in, then sealed

Shea butter, known locally as **ori** in Yoruba and **okwuma** in Igbo, is a popular sealant and is easy to find in Nigerian markets. Use a small amount, warmed between the palms. Too much butter on low porosity hair sits on top and attracts dust.
Relaxed hair needs the same moisture

Relaxed hair is chemically straightened, so it is more porous and weaker at the line where new growth meets relaxed hair. It still needs regular washing, conditioning and moisture. Be extra gentle at that line of demarcation, and avoid heavy heat.
Protecting hair between washes

Moisture escapes most at night, when cotton pillowcases rub the hair and soak up products. Cover the hair with a **satin or silk scarf or bonnet**, or sleep on a satin pillowcase. Between washes, lightly mist the ends with water or a leave-in spray and seal with a little oil every two or three days, or whenever the hair feels dry and stiff. Avoid tight rubber bands with metal joins; use soft scrunchies or fabric ties instead.

Cleaning is not the same as disinfecting
**Cleaning** removes hair, product and dirt with soap or detergent and water. You must clean first, because disinfectant cannot work through grease and hair.
**Disinfecting** kills most germs on a hard, clean surface using a chemical disinfectant left on for the full contact time stated on the label.
**Sterilising** kills all microbes and needs special equipment such as an autoclave. It is used in clinics, not usually in braiding salons.

Disinfectant only works on tools that are already clean.
Remove hair from combs and brushes straight after the client leaves.
Wash tools in warm water with liquid soap or detergent, scrubbing between the teeth with an old toothbrush.
Rinse and fully immerse them in a salon disinfectant (for example Barbicide) mixed exactly as the label says. Barbicide's label contact time is 10 minutes. For other products, follow their label.
Remove with gloves or tongs, rinse if the label says so, and air dry on a clean towel.
Store in a clean, closed container. Never put used tools back with clean ones.
Change the disinfectant solution as the label instructs, or sooner if it looks cloudy or has hair in it.
Using household bleach

If you use household bleach, dilute it exactly as the bottle instructs for disinfecting, mix a fresh batch each day, wear gloves, and work with a window open. Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other cleaners, because this releases dangerous gases. Do not soak metal scissors in bleach for long, as it can corrode them.
Your workstation and your hands

Wash your hands with soap and water before and after each client. Use a clean towel and cape for every client, and wash them with detergent before using again. Items that cannot be cleaned, such as cotton wool, used rubber bands and disposable neck strips, are thrown away after one client. Keep food and drinks off the work table, and keep chemicals out of children's reach.
Heat and hot water

Many braiders dip the ends of synthetic braids in hot water to seal them. Pour the water into a stable bowl or mug, never hold the kettle over the client, protect her shoulders and neck with a towel, and keep children well away. If you use a blow dryer, keep it moving, use a medium setting, and keep the cord away from water.

Cornrows are braids made flat against the scalp. In Nigeria they are often called **shuku** when they gather at the top, or all-back when they run from the front to the nape. They are the base skill for many other styles, including sew-in weaves and some wigs, so getting them neat and comfortable is worth practising until it feels natural.
A woman having her hair styled
Cornrows are a core skill: neat parts and steady hands matter more than speed at first.
Underhand versus overhand

A cornrow is a three-strand braid. In the **underhand** method, you cross the outer strands under the middle strand each time. This makes the braid stand up on top of the scalp, which is the classic cornrow look. In the **overhand** method, you cross over the middle, and the braid lies flatter and looks like a French braid. Most cornrows are done underhand.

Before you start
Hair should be clean, detangled, moisturised and stretched.
Have a rat-tail comb, clips, spray bottle and a light gel or braiding cream for grip.
Seat the client so her head is at your chest height. Bending for hours hurts your back and makes your rows uneven.
Decide the number of rows. For a beginner all-back style, 8 to 12 rows is manageable.
Braiding one row
With the tail of the comb, part a straight line from the front hairline to the nape. Part a second line parallel to it, the width you want the row. Clip the rest of the hair away.
Apply a little gel or cream along the row to control frizz and give grip.
At the hairline, take a small piece of hair and divide it into three equal strands: left, middle and right.
Cross the left strand under the middle. Now cross the right strand under the new middle. This is your first stitch.
Before each next cross, use your index finger to pick up a small amount of loose hair from the row just next to the strand, and add it to that outer strand. Then cross it under the middle.
Keep your hands close to the scalp and move along the row, adding hair each time, until you reach the nape.
When there is no more loose hair to pick up, continue a normal three-strand braid to the ends and secure with a small band or by twisting the ends.
Tension: firm, never painful

A cornrow should feel snug, not painful. If the client winces, if you see small white bumps, or if the scalp lifts like a tent around the base of the braid, the tension is too high. Pull hardest in the middle of the head and gentlest at the hairline and temples, where hair is finest. Dermatologists warn that repeated tight styling can lead to **traction alopecia**, hair loss from constant pulling, which can become permanent if it continues for years.

She wants 10 rows, so she divides 25 cm by 10: each row starts about 2.5 cm wide at the hairline.
She marks the centre part first, then works out to each side, so the rows on the left and right match.
Her first rows take about 12 minutes each. By row 6 she is down to about 8 minutes.

Esther finishes in about 2 hours, with rows matched on both sides because she started from the centre and measured.

Twists and box braids are among the most requested protective styles. **Protective styles** keep the ends of the hair tucked away and reduce daily combing, which can help retain length. They only protect the hair if they are not too tight, not too heavy and not left in too long.
A pair of scissors
Sharp scissors kept only for hair give clean, even ends on twists and braids.
Two-strand twists (natural hair, no extensions)
Start with clean, detangled, moisturised hair. Twists hold best on slightly damp hair with a twisting cream.
Part a small square section and comb it smooth.
Divide it into two equal strands.
Wrap one strand over the other, twisting each strand slightly in the same direction as you go, down to the ends.
Coil the ends around your finger to help them hold. Repeat across the head, working back to front or front to back in neat rows.
Box braids with extension hair

Box braids are three-strand braids that hang freely, with square or rectangular parts. Extension hair, usually a synthetic fibre such as pre-stretched braid hair, adds length and thickness. Knotless braids start with the client's own hair and add extension gradually with small feed-ins, so there is less weight on the root at the start.
Part the hair into rows, then part each row into squares of equal size. Use a ruler or your fingertip as a guide.
Take a piece of extension hair in proportion to the section. Too much extension on a small section pulls and can damage the root.

For a classic box braid, fold the extension around the base of the client's hair and braid three strands, keeping her hair mixed into two of them. For knotless, start braiding her own hair for two or three stitches, then feed in small pieces of extension.
Braid down to the length wanted with even tension.
Seal the ends: carefully dip synthetic ends in hot water from a stable bowl, then blot with a towel. Some fibres need a band or a twist instead.

Clients judge your work in two moments: when they look in the mirror on the day, and when they take the style down weeks later. Neat parts win the first moment. Healthy edges and a comfortable scalp win the second, and that is what brings them back and makes them recommend you.

Do the check standing back first, about an arm's length away, to see the overall shape. Then look closely at the hairline, the nape and behind the ears, the areas beginners rush. Ask the client to move her head side to side and look up and down, because tight braids often only hurt when she moves.
Traction alopecia: the damage to prevent

Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by repeated pulling on the hair roots. It usually shows first at the temples, the front hairline and around the ears. Early on it can recover if the pulling stops. If tight styles continue for a long time, the follicles can scar and the hair may not grow back. It is one of the most common causes of thin edges seen by dermatologists in women of African descent.
**Warning signs during or after styling**: pain, a stinging or burning feeling, headaches, small bumps or pimples at the base of braids, scalp lifting like a tent around the braid, and redness.
**Longer-term signs**: thinning or receding edges, short broken hairs along the hairline, and shiny patches where hair no longer grows.
**Higher-risk combinations**: tight braids on relaxed hair, heavy extensions on small sections, the same tight ponytail or bun every day, and glue-on hair applied to the hairline.
"It will loosen" is not an answer

Never send a client home with braids that hurt and tell her the pain will pass. If a braid hurts, loosen or redo it. Pain is the hair root being pulled, and the damage builds every day the style stays in.

Relaxers are still common in Nigerian salons. They permanently straighten afro-textured hair by breaking bonds inside the cortex. Because they are strong alkaline chemicals, they can cause scalp burns, eye injuries and severe breakage when used wrongly. This lesson gives you the core safety rules. Before you offer relaxers as a paid service, train with an experienced stylist and always follow the manufacturer's instructions for the exact product you use.
A yellow warning sign
Relaxers are strong alkaline chemicals: treat every application as a safety procedure.
Lye and no-lye relaxers
Lye vs no-lye relaxers
Lye relaxer
No-lye relaxer
Active: sodium hydroxide
Works fast
Higher risk of scalp burns
Rinses clean with neutraliser
Active: guanidine or calcium hydroxide
Often gentler on scalp
Can leave calcium build-up
Can feel drying on hair
No-lye does not mean no chemical: both are strong alkalis that need the same care.

**Lye relaxers** use sodium hydroxide, the same caustic soda used in soap making. **No-lye relaxers** usually use guanidine hydroxide (made by mixing calcium hydroxide cream with a guanidine carbonate activator) or another hydroxide. No-lye products are often marketed as milder for the scalp, but they can leave mineral deposits that make hair dry and dull unless washed out with a chelating shampoo. Both can burn and both can break hair.
Safety steps for a relaxer retouch

**Consult and check the scalp.** Do not relax if there are cuts, sores, scratches, irritation or a recent hair loss problem. Ask the client not to scratch, brush hard or wash her scalp for a day or two before the appointment.
**Strand test.** Follow the product's instructions to test a small hidden section, to see how the hair responds and how long it needs.
**Protect yourself and the client.** Wear gloves, put a cape and towel on the client, and protect her hairline, ears and scalp with a petroleum base cream.
**Apply only to new growth.** Relax only the untreated new growth, not the hair that was relaxed before. Overlapping onto old relaxed hair causes breakage.
**Time it exactly.** Use a timer and never exceed the time on the label. If the client says it burns, rinse immediately, do not wait.
**Rinse thoroughly and neutralise.** Rinse with plenty of lukewarm water, then use the neutralising shampoo that comes with the kit, repeating as the instructions say, until all relaxer is gone.
**Condition and record.** Apply conditioner, then record the product, timing and any reactions on the client card.
Eyes and burns

If relaxer gets into the eyes, rinse immediately with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help. If the scalp burns or blisters, rinse at once with lots of water and advise a clinic visit. Keep relaxers locked away from children.

Most stylists space relaxer retouches about 8 to 10 weeks apart or longer, and avoid colouring and relaxing on the same day. Many advise waiting about two weeks between a relaxer and colour, and between a relaxer and tight braids, so the scalp and hair can recover.
Health questions from clients

In 2022, the US National Institutes of Health reported a study that linked frequent use of chemical hair straighteners with a higher risk of uterine cancer. Studies like this show an association, not proof that relaxers cause cancer. If a client asks, share that research exists, do not make medical claims, and respect her choice to go natural or keep relaxing.
Consent, fairness and privacy
**Informed consent**: before a chemical service, explain the risks in plain words and let her decide. Write "risks explained, client agreed" on the card with the date.
**Children**: do not apply relaxers or chemical straighteners to children as part of this basic course's services.
**Fair treatment**: give every client the same quality and honesty, whatever her age, size, hair texture or ability to pay.
**Privacy**: keep client cards safe, and only post photos she has agreed to, with her face hidden if she prefers.
Handling a complaint
Listen fully without interrupting, and look at the problem together in good light.
If it is a safety issue (pain, burning, bumps, blisters), fix it or refer to a clinic first, before discussing money.
If the style has a fault you caused, such as uneven braids or a loose row, offer to redo that part free.
Record the complaint and what you did on the client card, so you learn from it.

For example, Adaeze in Owerri has a regular client, Nkem, booked for a relaxer retouch. During the consultation, Nkem mentions she scratched her scalp a lot last night because of dandruff.
Adaeze parts the hair and sees small scratch marks and redness near the crown.
She explains that relaxer on scratched skin can cause a painful burn.
She offers a gentle wash, conditioning treatment and a simple twist-out today instead, for her normal wash price.
She rebooks the relaxer for one week later and advises Nkem not to scratch, and to see a pharmacist or doctor about the dandruff if it continues.
Nkem leaves with clean, styled hair and no burn. She trusts Adaeze more because she put her safety ahead of the bigger sale.

Read your report once a month and ask three questions. Which style earns the most per hour? Where do my new clients come from? What one problem showed up more than once? Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are common. Before a client leaves, confirm the money in your own banking app. Never share your PIN, OTP or card details with anyone who calls claiming to be your bank.

A portfolio is your proof. New clients cannot feel how gentle your hands are or check your hygiene before they book, but they can see clean parts, healthy edges and neat ends in good photos. Your capstone project for this course is a portfolio of real work, with the records behind it.

Use daylight from a window or outdoors in the shade. Avoid direct midday sun, which creates harsh shadows, and avoid yellow bulbs at night.
Use a plain background: a clean wall or a sheet of plain fabric.
Clean the camera lens with a soft cloth before every session.
Take the same angles every time: front, left side, right side, back, and a close-up of the parts and hairline.
Hold the phone at the height of the hair, not from above, and tap the screen on the hair to focus.

Consent and privacy

Messy backgrounds such as unmade beds, kitchen pots or other people in the frame.
Photos taken only from the front, which hide the back where most uneven parts show.
Blurry close-ups because the lens was dirty or the phone moved.
Photos of styles you did not do, or styles copied from the internet. This is dishonest and clients will notice when your work looks different.
No record behind the photo: without the client card, time and finish check, a photo alone does not prove safe, repeatable work.

Pricing too low is one of the most common reasons small salons struggle. A low price fills your diary but leaves you tired and broke, and it can make clients doubt your quality. A good price covers your materials, your share of costs, and a fair pay for your hours, and still makes sense in your local market.
A bag of money
Your price must pay for materials, costs and your time, not just the products.
A simple pricing formula
**Materials**: everything used on that client (gel, cream, bands, extension hair if you supply it).
**Overhead share**: your monthly costs (disinfectant, linen washing, data, transport, tool replacement, rent if any) divided by the number of clients you expect.
**Your time**: hours the style takes multiplied by the hourly pay you want.
**Add them together** to get your minimum price. Then compare with what good stylists near you charge, and round to a clear figure.

Afro-textured hair is not hard or bad hair. The part you see is dead protein called keratin, so once it is damaged, it cannot heal. Prevention is everything.
On tightly coiled hair, the scalp's natural oil, sebum, struggles to travel past each bend, so the ends stay dry.
Every bend is a weak point. Combed dry, pulled tight or brushed hard, hair snaps there.
So keep three rules: moisture, gentle detangling, and low tension.

Wash about once every one to two weeks. Step one. Divide the hair into four to six sections, to prevent matting.
Step two. Shampoo the scalp with the pads of your fingers, not your nails, and let the lather run down the length.
Step three. Put conditioner on the length and ends, and leave it for the time on the label.
Step four. Detangle while the conditioner is still in. Fingers first, then a wide-tooth comb.
This is the rule. Start at the ends and work up to the roots. Never comb coily hair dry.
Step five. Rinse with cool or lukewarm water, then blot with a cotton T-shirt instead of rubbing.
Step six. Moisturise and seal. Water is the true moisturiser; oils and butters slow water loss.
LOC means liquid, then oil, then cream. Low porosity hair often prefers LCO, with oil last.

Step by step
Braiding one all-back row
Pick up a small, equal amount of hair on every cross.
Part two straight lines, front to nape
Add a little gel or cream for grip
Take a small piece, split into three strands
Cross left under middle, then right under
Add loose hair to the outer strand each time
Hands close to the scalp, all the way down
Start with clean, moisturised, stretched hair, and the client's head at your chest height.
Step one. With the comb tail, part a straight line from the hairline to the nape, then a second line parallel to it. Clip the rest away.
Step two. A little gel or braiding cream along the row controls frizz and gives grip.
Step three. At the hairline, take a small piece and divide it into three equal strands.
Step four. Cross the left strand under the middle, then the right strand under the new middle. This underhand method makes the classic raised cornrow.
Step five. Before each cross, pick up a little loose hair from the row with your index finger and add it to the outer strand.
Keep those amounts small and equal. Picking up too much is why rows get wider towards the nape.
Step six. Keep your knuckles close to the scalp to avoid gaps and loops. At the nape, finish with a normal three-strand braid and secure the end.

A cornrow should feel snug. Pull hardest in the middle of the head, and be gentlest at the hairline and temples, where hair is finest.
If she winces, if you see small white bumps, or the scalp lifts like a tent around the braid, it is too tight. Loosen it.

Before she leaves
Braids the same size
Clients judge your work twice: in the mirror on the day, and when they take the style down weeks later. Healthy edges win that second moment, and that is what brings them back.
So before she leaves, check six things. Parts straight. Braids the same size. No pain. Edges not pulled. Ends neat and sealed. Scalp clean.
Stand back an arm's length first, then look closely at the hairline, nape and behind the ears. Ask her to move her head, because tight braids often only hurt when she moves.
Prevent traction alopecia
Mistakes that damage hair
Very tight edges for a sleek look
Heavy extensions on small sections
Styles left in three months or more
"The pain will pass"
Do instead
Lighter tension, leave baby hairs out
Match extension to section size
Take down within four to eight weeks
Loosen or redo it now

Traction alopecia is hair loss from repeated pulling. It shows first at the temples and front hairline. Early on it can recover, but if pulling continues, follicles can scar and the hair may not grow back.
These are the habits that cause it.
Use lighter tension at the front. Match extension hair to the size of the section. Advise takedown within about four to eight weeks.
And never send a client home with braids that hurt. Pain is the root being pulled. Loosen or redo it.
Relaxer retouch
Relaxer safety, step by step
Never relax over cuts, scratches or irritation.
Consult and check the scalp
Strand test as the product says
Gloves on; base cream on hairline and ears
Apply only to new growth
Time it exactly; if it burns, rinse now
Rinse, neutralise fully, condition, record
Lye and no-lye relaxers are both strong alkalis that can burn. Train with an experienced stylist first, and follow the exact product's instructions.
Step one. Consult and check the scalp.
If there are cuts, sores, scratches or irritation, do not relax. Ask clients not to scratch or brush hard for a day or two before.
Step two. Do a strand test on a small hidden section.
Step three. Wear gloves, cape the client, and protect her hairline, ears and scalp with a petroleum base cream.
Step four. Apply only to new growth. Overlapping onto old relaxed hair causes breakage.
Step five. Use a timer and never pass the label time. If she says it burns, rinse immediately.
Step six. Rinse with plenty of lukewarm water, neutralise until all relaxer is gone, condition, and record the product and timing on her card.

Rinse at once with clean running water for at least 15 minutes. Get medical help.

Know your numbers
Profit per service: price minus materials
Earnings per hour: profit divided by hours
Repeat rate: repeat clients over all clients
Client sources: how new clients found you
Many talented braiders are always busy but never have money. Write one line in a log after every client: style, hours, price, materials, payment and source.
Profit per service is the price minus materials.
Earnings per hour is profit divided by hours. This shows which styles truly pay.
Repeat rate is repeat clients divided by all clients in the month. If it rises, clients trust you.
And count how new clients found you, so your effort goes where it works.

Your proof
Portfolio photos with a phone
Ask permission before every photo, and again before you post.
Daylight, not midday sun or yellow bulbs
Plain wall or plain fabric behind
Clean the lens before every session
Front, both sides, back, hairline close-up
Before set and a day-7 photo too
New clients cannot feel how gentle your hands are, but they can see clean parts and healthy edges in good photos.
Use daylight from a window, or outdoors in the shade.
Use a plain background. No unmade beds, kitchen pots or other people in the frame.
Clean the lens with a soft cloth, so close-ups are not blurry.
Take the same angles every time: front, left, right, back, and a close-up of the parts and hairline. The back is where uneven parts show.
Take a before set too. A photo a week later is powerful, because it shows your style stays neat and the hairline is calm.
Always ask permission, write the answer on her card, and hide faces when asked. For children, ask the parent and never show the child's face publicly.
Step by step
Know your minimum price and do not go below it.
Materials used on that client
Overhead share: monthly costs over clients
Your time: hours times the hourly pay you want
Add them up, then check local prices
Pricing too low is one of the most common reasons small salons struggle. A low price fills your diary but leaves you tired and broke.
First, count materials: gel, cream, bands, and extension hair if you supply it.
Second, your overhead share. Add your monthly costs like disinfectant, washing, data and transport, and divide by the clients you expect.
Third, your time. Hours the style takes, multiplied by the hourly pay you want.
Add them together. That is your minimum price. Then compare with good stylists near you, at least five of them, and round to a clear figure.
Below that minimum, you are paying to work.

On WhatsApp
Presenting your service
One sentence on what makes you different
Proof: before and after, day-7 photo
Easy booking: price, deposit, account, location
Clear rules: lateness, cancellations, inclusions
WhatsApp Business is a free app with a profile and a catalogue of services. Say what makes you different in one sentence, like: neat, gentle braids with clean tools for every client.
Show proof, and post one photo a few times a week rather than ten at once.
Make booking easy with the price, any deposit, your account details and location.
And be clear about your rules. If a client says the price is too high, do not argue. Offer a smaller option, like bigger braids or shorter length.
Protect your business
Three habits as you grow
Check every transfer and deposit in your own banking app, not a screenshot.
No edited photos, no styles you did not do, no claims that products make hair grow.
Clean tools after every client, no painful braids, no chemicals without checks and consent.
For long styles, a small deposit protects your time. Confirm it, and every transfer, in your own banking app.
Write honest captions. Never post styles you did not do. Clients will notice when your work looks different.
And as you get busy, keep the rules: tools cleaned after every client, no styling over infection, no painful braids, and no chemical service without a scalp check, strand test and consent.
